items.text: REFERRED TO INVESTIGATIONS AND GOVERNMENT OPERATIONS
COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO RULES
REFERRED TO CULTURAL AFFAIRS, TOURISM, PARKS AND RECREATION
COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO INVESTIGATIONS AND GOVERNMENT OPERATIONS

items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5525

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the arts and cultural affairs law, in relation to the
resale of tickets to places of entertainment; and to repeal certain
provisions of such law relating thereto


 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF THE BILL :
To put in place a price cap on tickets that are resold in order to
keep prices affordable for New Yorkers.

 SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS :
* Mandate disclosures before or at the time of sale of how many
tickets will actually be released to the general public.
* Require information on any obstructions or other limitations for
particular seats be posted.
* Limit ticket resales to no more than 25% above the face price of a
ticket
* Ban producers, promoters and their employees from engaging in
scalping or otherwise benefiting from the secondary market resales.
* Ban the resale of tickets until one month after the initial sale.
* Increases the fines for violating the law.

 JUSTIFICATION :

Two years ago the laws regulating ticket resale in New York State were
amended and the price cap at which tickets could be resold was
abolished. Eliminating the price cap was an unsuccessful endeavor and
needs to be changed. I will be introducing legislation that reinstates
a price cap. This proposal does not mean a producer or owner of a
venue cannot charge what they want. Instead this bill focuses on the
middlemen who are reaping exorbitant fees at the expense of the
average person who can no longer afford to buy tickets. Recent events
with hugely inflated ticket prices for Hannah Montana/Miley Cyrus and
the Springsteen ticket sale debacle provide ample evidence of a
dysfunctional marketplace in which consumers either lose out or pay
astronomical amounts to see their favorite live events. This
legislation will put a stop to that practice.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
New bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
Not applicable.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.
